title: Research Question to Method Mapper
summary: Three fictional research questions, read twice each: what kind of answer the wording asks for, and what kind of study could produce it. There is no answer key, options carry three standings rather than two, and the third question is deliberately unsettled.
learningObjectives: Read a research question for what would count as an answer to it, before considering any method.
Distinguish description, difference, association, explanation, interpretation and prediction as aims.
Explain why the aim of a question constrains whether qualitative, quantitative or mixed material could answer it.
Recognise that more than one reading of a question can be defensible, and say what each would commit the researcher to.
Identify a question whose wording does not settle the method, and say what commitment would have to be made instead.
interactionTypes: sequential cases read in two parts
three-level standing rather than right or wrong
explanatory note on every option whether chosen or not
a deliberately unsettled question the activity refuses to resolve
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. Answered options are marked aria-disabled rather than disabled so they stay in the tab order and can be re-read. The three standings are signalled by border style and a glyph as well as by colour, and each carries a visually hidden sentence naming it. Every option has a written note whether or not it was chosen. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Fictional. All three questions, samples and settings are invented for teaching.
simulationNotes: Each option for each question carries a standing: strong means well supported by the wording as written, defensible means the note says what it would commit you to, and the remainder are hard to defend from this wording. These are one experienced reading rather than an answer key. Question 3 is deliberately unsettled: explanation and interpretation are both strong, and all three of qualitative, quantitative and mixed are strong, and the activity says so rather than picking a winner. No statistical test is named anywhere, because the reasoning that stops before the test is the part students most often skip.
readmeTopic: reading a research question for what would count as an answer
